candidate.educational_objective: Address safety-relevant informational conflict by explicitly sharing the differing information, seeking review/acknowledgment, and escalating appropriately if the concern remains unresolved.

options.A: Avoid discussing the disagreement so each nurse can follow a separate plan during their own shift, even if care becomes inconsistent.
options.B: Have the more senior nurse decide without reviewing the other nurse’s concern because hierarchy is the preferred response to informational conflict.
options.C: Begin formal disciplinary action against one nurse before attempting a structured safety discussion because clinical disagreement itself is misconduct.
options.D: Use a structured safety discussion to state the differing clinical information, seek acknowledgment and review, and escalate through the team if the safety concern remains unresolved so one patient-centered plan is established.

candidate.rationale: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS defines informational conflict as disagreement involving different information related to the task or care plan. It specifically identifies the Two-Challenge Rule as a tool when team members have different information; if the concern persists, the challenger can escalate through the chain of command. D addresses the informational conflict while preserving one patient-centered plan.
candidate.source_claim_supported: TeamSTEPPS treats differing clinical information as informational conflict and supports structured assertion/review with escalation when a safety concern is not resolved.

candidate.stem: Two nurses disagree about how aggressively to mobilize a client who recently fell. Both have clinically relevant but different information, and the disagreement is beginning to affect the care plan. Which approach is most appropriate?
